title: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02)

intro.about: The AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) is AWS's foundational certification: it validates that a candidate can explain the value of the AWS Cloud, work with the shared responsibility model and core security and compliance concepts, recognize what the principal AWS services do, and reason about pricing, billing and support channels — all at recognition level, without designing, building or troubleshooting anything. The exam guide defines four content domains: Cloud Concepts (24%), Security and Compliance (30%), Cloud Technology and Services (34%), and Billing, Pricing, and Support (12%).
intro.audience: Aimed at people who need a working vocabulary of the AWS Cloud rather than hands-on depth — the exam guide targets candidates with up to about six months of exposure to AWS, explicitly including non-IT backgrounds. That fits sales, marketing, finance, project-management, procurement and leadership roles working around AWS teams, and it is the common first rung for career changers heading toward the associate-level certifications. Items reward recognition, positioning and selection; coding, architecture design, troubleshooting and implementation are declared out of scope by the guide.

materials.title: 50-question practice form
materials.description: Weighted to the official exam guide across all four domains and drawn from a 68-item originally-authored bank — the same size as the real exam's scored portion (AWS adds 15 unscored pretest questions this mock does not simulate).

materials.title: Two question formats, matching the real exam exactly
materials.description: Multiple choice (one key among four options) and multiple response (pick two of five) — the only two item types CLF-C02 uses, so every question mechanic you meet here also appears on the real exam. The format note below records the two calibration caveats behind that claim.

materials.title: Review dashboard and rationales
materials.description: Per-domain scoring against a 70% threshold (a raw-score proxy for the real exam's scaled 700-of-1,000 pass mark), plus an explanation for the key and every distractor on submission, written in the exam guide's own vocabulary.

intro.disclaimer: An independent, originally-authored study tool for personal exam preparation — not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to Amazon Web Services, Inc. or Pearson VUE. AWS, Amazon Web Services and AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner are trademarks of Amazon.com, Inc. or its affiliates. Every question was written clean-room from documented derivation artefacts against the public exam guide, with prior practice sets analyzed for classification only, exactly as this package's source registry and derivation records show. Nothing here is drawn from the live CLF-C02 item bank: real exam content is confidential and protected by the AWS Certification NDA, which binds you too once you sit the exam — please never share live questions here.

format_coverage: The real CLF-C02 exam uses exactly two item types: multiple choice (one correct response and three distractors) and multiple response (two or more correct responses among five or more response options). The exam guide names no other type. Both map 1:1 onto Mockka formats, so this mock reproduces 100% of the exam's item types — the exam's formats are a strict subset of Mockka's three. Mockka's third format, scenario_matching, is NOT a CLF-C02 item type and is set to 0 in every domain; it must not be used for this exam. Two fidelity caveats stand: (1) the blueprint permits multiple-response items with more than two keys and more than five options, but all 80 items across the three registered practice sources are choose-2-of-5, so the corpus supplies no calibration for wider items — the select_count and options values above are the corpus's shape, not the blueprint's ceiling, and S3 owns that decision; (2) the blueprint states no proportion of multiple-response items, and the practice sources disagree (14%, 23%, 30%), so the per-domain format_mix is a documented authoring judgment rather than a measured value.
